body.heading: An acid meets a base
paragraphs: Vinegar is a mild acid — acetic acid in water. Baking soda is a gentle base, sodium bicarbonate. Put them together and they do what acids and bases do: they neutralise each other.

The drama comes from a by-product. The reaction releases carbon dioxide gas, and that gas is the fizz — thousands of bubbles racing to escape. What is left behind is mostly water and a harmless salt called sodium acetate.

body.heading: The same gas lifts your cakes
paragraphs: This is not just a party trick; it is how baking works. In a cake batter, baking soda meets something acidic — buttermilk, yoghurt, lemon juice, cocoa — and the carbon dioxide bubbles inflate the mixture as it sets in the oven.
Baking powder is the self-contained version: it carries its own powdered acid, so it only needs moisture and heat to start bubbling.

body.heading: A fair test to try
paragraphs: The classic volcano hides a good experiment. Fix the amount of baking soda and vary the vinegar, and the fizz grows — but only up to a point. Past that point, extra vinegar changes nothing, because the soda has run out.
Chemists call the ingredient that runs out first the limiting reactant. Your kitchen volcano just demonstrated a concept that runs factories and pharmacies alike.

takeaway: The famous fizz is carbon dioxide escaping as an acid and a base neutralise each other — the same gas that lifts your cakes.
